questions.q: What is the primary goal of an SSRF attack against a cloud server?
options: To crash the web application
To brute-force the login page
To trick the server into making requests the attacker chooses, often to reach internal services like the metadata endpoint
To encrypt the server's files for ransom
questions.explanation: SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery) tricks the server itself into fetching a URL the attacker chose, often reaching internal-only services the attacker could never reach directly.

questions.q: Which internal IP address hosts the cloud instance metadata service (IMDS) across AWS, Azure, and GCP?
questions.explanation: All three major cloud providers use the same reserved link-local address, 169.254.169.254, only reachable from inside the machine itself.

questions.q: An app blocks http:// URLs in its SSRF-vulnerable feature but still allows file://. What can an attacker read to potentially find leaked cloud credentials?
options: /etc/hostname
/proc/self/environ
/var/log/syslog
/tmp/cache.db
questions.explanation: The process environment file holds every environment variable a process started with, which is often exactly where cloud credentials get injected in serverless and container deployments.

questions.q: Why does IMDSv2 resist basic SSRF attacks better than IMDSv1?
options: It uses a completely different, unguessable IP address
It requires a special header and a two-step token request that most simple SSRF bugs cannot add
It is only accessible from a VPN
It disables all metadata access permanently
questions.explanation: IMDSv2 requires first fetching a token using a custom header, and most basic SSRF vulnerabilities cannot forge custom headers on the request they trigger.

questions.q: In IAM, what does the 'AssumeRole' action allow an identity to do?
options: Delete another role permanently
Reset a user's password
Create a brand-new cloud account
Temporarily borrow another role's identity and permissions
questions.explanation: AssumeRole lets an identity temporarily take on a different role's permissions, similar to picking up a different keycard for a while.

questions.q: What does the 'PassRole' technique allow an attacker to do?
options: Directly steal another user's password
Attach a powerful role to a new service (like a notebook) they control, so their code runs with that role's permissions
Force another user to log out
Bypass multi-factor authentication entirely
questions.explanation: PassRole lets you hand a powerful role to a service you control, like building a robot and giving it a manager's badge — your code then runs with that role's power.

questions.q: Why is a wildcard (*) in an IAM policy's Action or Resource field considered dangerous?
options: It slows down every API call significantly
It only affects billing, not security
It grants access to everything matching that field, often far more than intended
It requires additional encryption keys
questions.explanation: A wildcard means "everything" — a policy with s3:* and Resource: * can touch every S3 bucket in the account, including ones from completely unrelated projects.

questions.q: Why are failed training jobs an especially good place to hunt for credentials?
options: They run faster than successful jobs
They automatically encrypt all secrets
They delete all logs immediately
Error handlers often dump environment variables and secrets, and nobody reviews failed runs
questions.explanation: When something breaks, error handlers frequently print out the full environment for debugging — and since the job failed, few people ever go back and review those logs.

questions.q: What is the danger of storing an AWS SSM parameter as plain 'String' instead of 'SecureString'?
options: String parameters cost more money
String parameters are stored and returned as plaintext, with no encryption protecting the value
String parameters cannot hold more than 10 characters
String parameters are automatically shared with other AWS accounts
questions.explanation: SecureString values are encrypted; plain String values are stored and returned as plaintext, meaning anyone who can read the parameter sees the secret directly.

questions.q: What firewall rule value means a port is open to the entire internet?
questions.explanation: 0.0.0.0/0 matches every possible IP address, meaning literally anyone on the internet can reach that port.

questions.q: Why is discovering a model server's exact version number (e.g. via a /version endpoint) valuable to an attacker?
options: It lets them change the server's hostname
It reveals the exact software build, which can then be checked against known CVEs for that version
It automatically grants admin access
It disables the server's rate limiting
questions.explanation: Once the exact version is known, an attacker can search for publicly known vulnerabilities (CVEs) affecting that specific build.

questions.q: In Kubernetes, why is the ability to 'create pods' effectively equal to cluster admin?
options: Because creating pods deletes the audit logs
Because pods automatically become the cluster owner
Because you can launch a pod that mounts the host filesystem or runs as a more powerful service account
Because it disables all RBAC rules
questions.explanation: A pod you create can be configured to mount the host's filesystem or run with a stronger service account, effectively handing you control of the whole cluster.

questions.q: What is the difference between a Kubernetes Role and a ClusterRole?
options: A Role only works for humans, a ClusterRole only for pods
A Role applies to one namespace only; a ClusterRole applies across the entire cluster
There is no functional difference between them
A ClusterRole expires automatically after 24 hours
questions.explanation: A Role is scoped to a single namespace, while a ClusterRole's permissions apply cluster-wide, across every namespace.

questions.q: What is 'identity chaining' in a Kubernetes attack?
options: Linking multiple user passwords together
Rotating tokens every hour automatically
Encrypting service account tokens
Combining a read-only identity to steal a more powerful identity's token, gaining capabilities neither had alone
questions.explanation: An identity that can only read secrets uses that ability to read a stronger identity's stored token, effectively becoming that stronger identity.

questions.q: Which single YAML setting removes the most common Kubernetes lateral-movement path by not mounting a token into a pod?
options: privileged: true
automountServiceAccountToken: false
hostNetwork: true
replicas: 0
questions.explanation: This setting stops Kubernetes from automatically placing a service account token into a pod that doesn't need to talk to the Kubernetes API at all.

questions.q: Why are legacy (pre-v1.24) Kubernetes service account tokens considered a bigger risk than modern bound tokens?
options: Legacy tokens are shorter and easier to guess
Legacy tokens never expire, so a stolen one remains valid indefinitely
Legacy tokens can only be used once
Legacy tokens require a password in addition
questions.explanation: Legacy tokens have no expiration at all, so once stolen, they keep working forever unless manually revoked. Bound tokens expire quickly and are audience-restricted.

questions.q: How can a compromised pre-processing sidecar container break a model's results without ever touching the model itself?
options: By modifying requests in a shared volume before the model reads them
By directly editing the model's weight files
By changing the model's version number
By disabling the model's GPU access
questions.explanation: Since containers in the same pod share volumes, a compromised sidecar can quietly rewrite the data flowing through a shared queue before the model ever sees it.

questions.q: In the GPU container escape (CVE-2025-23266), what role does the LD_PRELOAD environment variable play?
options: It disables GPU access entirely
It forces the dynamic linker to load the attacker's malicious library first, running its code as root on the host
It encrypts the container's filesystem
It only affects network settings
questions.explanation: LD_PRELOAD tells the system to load a specific library before anything else. Chained with the runc and toolkit bugs, this results in the attacker's code running as root on the host.

questions.q: Why do simple Docker wrapper scripts that block flags like --privileged fail to stop the CVE-2025-23266 GPU escape?
options: The exploit hides in the Dockerfile's ENV directive, not in any command-line flag the wrapper checks
The wrapper scripts are always disabled by default
The exploit only works on Windows containers
GPU exploits cannot be blocked by any wrapper
questions.explanation: The malicious LD_PRELOAD is baked into the image itself via an ENV directive, so a wrapper that only inspects command-line flags never sees it.

questions.q: What is the single most powerful principle for defending AI infrastructure across cloud, Kubernetes, and containers?
options: Using the longest possible passwords
Turning off all logging to reduce noise
Running everything as root for simplicity
Least privilege — giving every identity only the permissions it truly needs
questions.explanation: Least privilege alone closes off most of the escalation paths covered in this module — wildcard IAM policies, overly broad RBAC, and unnecessary create-pod permissions all stem from violating it.
